about: CEGE0108 is a compulsory 15-credit (FHEQ Level 4) first-year module for UCL Civil Engineering students, taught in person across Terms 1 and 2 by the Department of Civil, Environmental and Geomatic Engineering. It covers the fundamentals of applied fluid mechanics (forces on fluids, continuity, hydrostatics, Bernoulli and the steady-flow energy equation for pipes) and of engineering materials (mechanical behaviour, metals, polymers and ceramics, and timber), and it links to the first-year civil engineering design module. In the 2026/27 module catalogue it is assessed by an exam (70%), group activity (25%, three assessments) and in-class activity (5%). The topics below follow the learning outcomes listed in the catalogue, which does not give a week-by-week order.
topics: Forces on fluids and basic fluid motion
Energy conservation and the Bernoulli equation
Steady-flow energy equation for pipes and pipelines
Mechanical behaviour I: elastic and plastic deformation, mechanical testing
Mechanical behaviour II: fracture, impact, creep and fatigue
Structure and properties of metals, polymers and ceramics
Timber: composition, mechanical behaviour and durability

notes.h: What a fluid is, the forces on it, and how flow is described
notes.body:
A fluid is a substance that deforms continuously under any shear stress, however small. A solid can resist a shear stress by deforming a finite amount and then stopping. It follows that a fluid at rest carries no shear stress at all: the only surface force in a static fluid is pressure.

- Liquids such as water are almost incompressible (the bulk modulus of water is roughly 2.2 GPa), so their density is treated as constant.
- Gases are compressible, but at low speeds (Mach number below about 0.3) they can also be treated as incompressible.

Forces on a fluid volume
Picture a small control volume of fluid. The forces on it fall into two groups:
- Body forces act on the whole mass. In civil engineering this is almost always gravity, ρg per unit volume.
- Surface forces act on the boundary: pressure (normal to the surface and compressive) and shear stress (tangential, caused by viscosity).
In a fluid at rest only gravity and pressure act, which gives hydrostatics. In a moving fluid, viscous shear and changes of momentum also matter.

Pressure
Pressure p is normal force per unit area (Pa = N/m²). At a point in a static fluid it has the same value in every direction (Pascal's law). Gauge pressure is measured relative to the local atmosphere (about 101.3 kPa at sea level); absolute pressure = gauge pressure + atmospheric pressure.

Viscosity
For a Newtonian fluid, Newton's law of viscosity is τ = μ du/dy, where μ is the dynamic viscosity (Pa s) and du/dy is the velocity gradient normal to the flow. Kinematic viscosity is ν = μ/ρ (m²/s). Approximate values for water at 20 °C: ρ ≈ 998 kg/m³ (1000 kg/m³ is used in most calculations), μ ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa s, ν ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s. The viscosity of liquids falls as temperature rises; that of gases rises.

The no-slip condition says that fluid in contact with a solid surface moves with that surface, so velocity gradients (and shear) are largest next to walls.

Worked example: a plate of area 0.5 m² slides at 0.5 m/s over a 2 mm film of oil with μ = 0.08 Pa s. With a linear velocity profile, τ = μU/h = 0.08 × 0.5 / 0.002 = 20 Pa, so the drag force is τA = 20 × 0.5 = 10 N.

Describing a flow
- Steady flow: conditions at a fixed point do not change with time. Unsteady flow: they do.
- Uniform flow: conditions are the same at every position along the flow at a given instant. Non-uniform flow: they change with position (for example through a taper).
- A streamline is a line everywhere tangent to the velocity, so no fluid crosses it. In steady flow, streamlines, pathlines and streaklines coincide.
- In one-dimensional analysis each cross-section is described by a single mean velocity V = Q/A.

Laminar and turbulent flow
Osborne Reynolds' dye experiments (1883) showed that pipe flow is laminar (smooth, layered) at low speeds and turbulent (eddying, strongly mixing) at higher speeds. The controlling group is the Reynolds number, the ratio of inertial to viscous forces:
Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν
Typical guide values for pipes are laminar below Re ≈ 2000, turbulent above about 4000, and transitional in between. Most water mains, sewers and rivers carry turbulent flow.

Exam tips: always convert millimetres to metres before using τ = μ du/dy or Re; state which viscosity (μ or ν) you are using; and when asked to classify a flow, quote the Re value and the threshold you are comparing it with.

notes.h: Conservation of mass: the continuity equation
notes.body:
The continuity equation is conservation of mass applied to a control volume. For steady flow, whatever mass enters must leave, because nothing can accumulate inside.

Mass flow rate: ṁ = ρAV (kg/s), where A is the cross-sectional area normal to the flow and V the mean velocity.
For steady flow between sections 1 and 2: ρ₁A₁V₁ = ρ₂A₂V₂.
For an incompressible fluid (water in almost every civil engineering problem) the density cancels and the volume flow rate (discharge) is constant:
Q = A₁V₁ = A₂V₂ (m³/s)

Mean velocity
The real velocity varies across a section (zero at the walls by the no-slip condition, maximum near the centre). V = Q/A is the mean velocity that gives the correct discharge, and it is the value used in 1D calculations.

Circular pipes
A = πD²/4, so V₂/V₁ = A₁/A₂ = (D₁/D₂)². Halving the diameter quadruples the velocity.
Worked example: a 300 mm pipe carrying water at 1.2 m/s reduces to 150 mm.
- Q = (π/4)(0.3)²(1.2) = 0.0848 m³/s (84.8 L/s)
- V₂ = V₁(D₁/D₂)² = 1.2 × 2² = 4.8 m/s

Junctions
At a junction, ΣQ in = ΣQ out. Example: a main carrying 0.10 m³/s splits into two branches. Branch 2 is 200 mm in diameter with mean velocity 2.0 m/s, so Q₂ = (π/4)(0.2)²(2.0) = 0.0628 m³/s. Branch 3 must carry Q₃ = 0.10 − 0.0628 = 0.0372 m³/s.

Open channels
For a rectangular channel of width b and depth y, A = by, so Q = byV. If a channel 4 m wide and 1.5 m deep flows at 0.8 m/s, Q = 4.8 m³/s. Where it narrows to 3 m wide and 1.2 m deep, V = 4.8/(3 × 1.2) = 1.33 m/s.

Unsteady problems: tanks and reservoirs
If a volume is filling or emptying, the difference between inflow and outflow becomes storage:
A_tank × dh/dt = Q_in − Q_out
Example: a tank with plan area 4 m² receives 0.05 m³/s and releases 0.02 m³/s, so the level rises at 0.03/4 = 0.0075 m/s (7.5 mm/s).

Why continuity matters
Continuity on its own gives velocities. It is then combined with the Bernoulli or energy equation to find pressures (Venturi meters, nozzles, tapers) and with the momentum equation to find forces. In almost every fluids exam question, continuity is the first line of working.

Common mistakes
- Using diameters in millimetres, or forgetting the factor of 4 in πD²/4.
- Scaling velocity by the diameter ratio instead of the area ratio (the square of the diameter ratio).
- Mixing litres and cubic metres: 1 m³/s = 1000 L/s.

Exam tips: write Q = AV explicitly at each section, draw the control volume with arrows for every inflow and outflow, and check that the narrowest section has the highest velocity before moving on.

notes.h: Hydrostatics: pressure, manometers and forces on submerged surfaces
notes.body:
Hydrostatics deals with fluids at rest, where only pressure and gravity act.

Pressure variation with depth
Equilibrium of a small vertical column gives dp/dz = −ρg (z measured upwards). For a liquid of constant density with free-surface pressure p₀:
p = p₀ + ρgh, where h is the depth below the surface.
Pressure depends only on depth, not on the shape of the container. Pressure head is h = p/(ρg).
Example: at 8 m depth in water, gauge pressure = 1000 × 9.81 × 8 = 78.5 kPa; absolute pressure ≈ 78.5 + 101.3 = 179.8 kPa.

Manometers
- A piezometer is a simple open tube: the liquid rises to a height p/(ρg).
- A U-tube manometer uses a denser liquid (often mercury, ρ ≈ 13 600 kg/m³) to measure larger pressures.
- A differential manometer measures the pressure difference between two points.
Method: start at one end, add ρgh when moving down through a fluid, subtract ρgh when moving up, and use the fact that points at the same level in the same continuous fluid have equal pressure.
Example: a water pipe is connected to a mercury U-tube open to air. The mercury in the open limb stands 0.25 m above the mercury interface in the pipe limb, and the pipe centre is 0.10 m above that interface. Then p_A + 1000g(0.10) = 13 600g(0.25), giving p_A = 33.35 − 0.98 = 32.4 kPa gauge.

Force on a plane surface
The resultant force is F = ρg h_c A, where h_c is the depth of the centroid of the area A. It acts at the centre of pressure, which is below the centroid because pressure increases with depth:
y_p = y_c + I_G/(y_c A)
where y is measured along the plane from the free surface (y = depth for a vertical surface) and I_G is the second moment of area about the horizontal axis through the centroid (bd³/12 for a rectangle).
Worked example: a vertical rectangular gate 2 m wide and 3 m high has its top edge 1 m below the water surface. h_c = 2.5 m and A = 6 m², so F = 1000 × 9.81 × 2.5 × 6 = 147 kN. I_G = 2 × 3³/12 = 4.5 m⁴, so y_p = 2.5 + 4.5/(2.5 × 6) = 2.8 m below the surface.
For simple rectangles you can also use the pressure prism: the force equals the volume of the pressure diagram, acting through its centroid.

Force on a curved surface
- Horizontal component = the force on the vertical projection of the surface, acting through that projection's centre of pressure.
- Vertical component = the weight of fluid (real or imaginary) between the surface and the free surface, acting through its centroid.
For a circular arc the resultant passes through the centre of curvature, because every pressure force is normal to the surface.

Buoyancy and floating
Archimedes' principle: the upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced and acts through the centroid of the displaced volume (the centre of buoyancy, B). A floating body displaces its own weight. Example: a timber block of density 600 kg/m³ and depth 0.4 m floats with a draught of (600/1000) × 0.4 = 0.24 m.
Stability: the metacentric height GM = BM − BG, with BM = I/V (I = second moment of the waterplane area about the tilt axis, V = displaced volume). The body is stable if M lies above G (GM > 0).

Exam tips: always state gauge or absolute; for gates, take moments about the hinge using the centre of pressure, not the centroid; for curved surfaces, sketch the vertical projection and the volume above the surface.

notes.h: Energy in a flowing fluid and the Bernoulli equation
notes.body:
Energy per unit weight of fluid is expressed as heads (metres):
- pressure head p/(ρg)
- velocity (kinetic) head V²/(2g)
- elevation (potential) head z
Their sum is the total head H. The sum of pressure head and elevation, p/(ρg) + z, is the piezometric head.

The Bernoulli equation
p/(ρg) + V²/(2g) + z = constant along a streamline
or equivalently p + ½ρV² + ρgz = constant.
It follows from Newton's second law applied along a streamline (Euler's equation) and holds only when:
- the flow is steady
- the fluid is incompressible
- the flow is inviscid (frictionless), so no energy is lost
- it is applied along a single streamline (or across streamlines if the flow is irrotational)
- no pump or turbine adds or removes energy and there is no heat transfer.
In pipe problems we apply it between two sections using mean velocities; when friction matters we add head losses (the steady-flow energy equation, next topic).

The trade-off it describes: where velocity rises, pressure must fall (at constant elevation). This explains flow meters, siphons and cavitation. The absolute pressure cannot fall below the vapour pressure of water (about 2.3 kPa at 20 °C) without vapour bubbles forming.

Applications
1. Flow from an orifice (Torricelli). Between the free surface of a large tank (V ≈ 0, p = 0 gauge) and the jet (p = 0 gauge), a depth h below: V = √(2gh). For h = 5 m, V = √(2 × 9.81 × 5) = 9.90 m/s. Real discharge is Q = C_d a √(2gh), where C_d = C_c × C_v (contraction × velocity coefficients). For a sharp-edged orifice C_d is roughly 0.6, mainly because the jet contracts to a vena contracta.

2. Pitot tube. At a stagnation point the fluid is brought to rest, so p₀ = p + ½ρV² and V = √(2(p₀ − p)/ρ). Example: air (ρ = 1.2 kg/m³) with p₀ − p = 300 Pa gives V = √(600/1.2) = 22.4 m/s.

3. Venturi meter. Continuity (A₁V₁ = A₂V₂) plus Bernoulli between the inlet and the throat gives
Q = C_d A₂ √( 2gΔh / (1 − (A₂/A₁)²) )
where Δh is the difference in piezometric head. With a mercury–water differential manometer reading x, Δh = x(ρ_Hg/ρ_w − 1) = 12.6x metres of water, whatever the meter's inclination.
Worked example: inlet 200 mm, throat 100 mm, x = 0.2 m of mercury. Δh = 0.2 × 12.6 = 2.52 m. A₂ = 7.854 × 10⁻³ m², (A₂/A₁)² = 1/16, so ideal Q = 7.854 × 10⁻³ × √(2 × 9.81 × 2.52 / (15/16)) = 0.0570 m³/s. A real meter has C_d close to 1 (roughly 0.95–0.99).

Kinetic energy correction factor
Because velocity varies across a section, the true kinetic energy flux is αV²/(2g). α is close to 1 (about 1.0–1.1) for turbulent pipe flow and 2 for laminar flow; it is usually taken as 1 in first-year problems.

Exam tips: list Bernoulli's assumptions whenever you use it; choose points 1 and 2 where you know most quantities (free surfaces, jets at atmospheric pressure); use continuity to link velocities; and convert manometer readings to metres of the flowing fluid before substituting.

notes.h: The steady-flow energy equation, pipe friction and pipelines
notes.body:
Real pipe flow loses mechanical energy to friction, and pumps or turbines may add or remove energy. The steady-flow energy equation (SFEE), in head form between sections 1 and 2, is:
p₁/(ρg) + V₁²/(2g) + z₁ + h_p = p₂/(ρg) + V₂²/(2g) + z₂ + h_t + h_L
where h_p is the head added by a pump, h_t the head taken out by a turbine and h_L the total head loss. It comes from the first law of thermodynamics: the "lost" head is mechanical energy turned into heat.

Friction loss: Darcy–Weisbach
h_f = f (L/D) V²/(2g)
where f is the dimensionless Darcy friction factor (written λ in many UK texts), L the pipe length and D the diameter.
Warning: some older texts write h_f = 4fLV²/(2gD) using the Fanning factor, which is a quarter of the Darcy value. Check which definition a question uses.
Worked example: L = 500 m, D = 0.2 m, V = 1.5 m/s, f = 0.02. h_f = 0.02 × (500/0.2) × 1.5²/(2 × 9.81) = 5.73 m.

Laminar flow (Re below about 2000)
f = 64/Re, which is the Hagen–Poiseuille result Δp = 32μLV/D² written in Darcy form. Example: oil (ρ = 900 kg/m³, μ = 0.1 Pa s) at 1 m/s in a 50 mm pipe: Re = 450, f = 0.142, and over 20 m h_f = 2.90 m of oil.

Turbulent flow
f depends on Re and the relative roughness k_s/D. The Colebrook–White equation is
1/√f = −2 log₁₀( k_s/(3.7D) + 2.51/(Re√f) )
It is implicit in f, so you iterate (start with f ≈ 0.02, substitute, repeat) or read the Moody diagram, which plots the same relationship. In the fully rough zone the Re term becomes negligible and f depends only on k_s/D. The Swamee–Jain formula, f = 0.25/[log₁₀(k_s/(3.7D) + 5.74/Re⁰·⁹)]², is a widely used explicit approximation. Roughness values are approximate and grow as pipes age.

Local (minor) losses
h_m = K V²/(2g)
- Sharp-edged entrance from a reservoir: K ≈ 0.5.
- Exit into a reservoir: K = 1.0 (the whole velocity head is lost).
- Sudden expansion: h_m = (V₁ − V₂)²/(2g).
- Valves and bends: K from manufacturers' or textbook tables.
In long pipelines friction usually dominates; in short pipes local losses can matter as much.

Energy and hydraulic grade lines
- The energy grade line (EGL) is at height p/(ρg) + V²/(2g) + z. It falls steadily along a uniform pipe, drops suddenly at local losses and rises at a pump.
- The hydraulic grade line (HGL) is at p/(ρg) + z, one velocity head below the EGL.
- Where the HGL drops below the pipe, the pressure is below atmospheric: a risk of air release, contamination or cavitation.

Pipelines
- Reservoir to reservoir: the difference in water levels equals the sum of all losses, which you solve for V and Q.
- Pipes in series: the same Q flows through each; losses add.
- Pipes in parallel: each branch has the same head loss; flows add.
- Pump power: P = ρgQH_p/η. Example: lifting 0.05 m³/s through 25 m with 3.5 m of losses at η = 0.75 needs 1000 × 9.81 × 0.05 × 28.5/0.75 = 18.6 kW.

Exam tips: write the SFEE between two clearly marked points (usually free surfaces), list every loss, and for turbulent flow check your assumed f against Re and k_s/D.

notes.h: Stress, strain, elasticity, plasticity and how materials are tested
notes.body:
Basic definitions
- Engineering stress σ = F/A₀ (A₀ = original area). 1 MPa = 1 N/mm².
- Engineering strain ε = ΔL/L₀ (dimensionless).
- Hooke's law in the elastic range: σ = Eε, where E is Young's modulus.
- Poisson's ratio ν = −(lateral strain)/(axial strain): about 0.3 for steel and about 0.2 for concrete.
- Shear modulus G = E/(2(1 + ν)) for an isotropic material.

Approximate stiffness values
- Steel: about 200–210 GPa (Eurocode 3 uses 210 GPa for structural steel; Eurocode 2 uses 200 GPa for reinforcing steel).
- Aluminium alloys: about 70 GPa.
- Concrete: about 30–40 GPa (C30/37 has E_cm ≈ 33 GPa in EN 1992-1-1).
- Softwood along the grain: about 7–14 GPa (C24 has E₀,mean = 11 GPa in EN 338).
- Polymers: roughly 0.2–4 GPa.

The tensile test (for metals, BS EN ISO 6892-1)
A typical mild steel curve shows:
- a linear elastic region up to the limit of proportionality;
- yielding, often with an upper and lower yield point and a yield plateau;
- strain hardening up to the ultimate tensile strength (UTS, the maximum engineering stress);
- necking, where deformation localises, and then fracture.
For metals without a clear yield point (aluminium, high-strength steels) the 0.2% proof stress is used: draw a line parallel to the elastic slope from 0.2% strain and read the stress where it meets the curve.
Ductility is reported as percentage elongation after fracture and percentage reduction of area.
True stress σ_T = σ(1 + ε) and true strain ε_T = ln(1 + ε) (valid up to the onset of necking).

Elastic and plastic deformation
Elastic strain is recoverable: atomic bonds stretch but no permanent rearrangement occurs. Plastic strain is permanent: in metals it happens by dislocation slip. If a specimen is unloaded after yielding, it unloads along a line parallel to the original elastic slope, leaving a permanent set.
- Resilience (elastic energy stored per unit volume up to yield) = σ_y²/(2E). For S355 steel: 355²/(2 × 210 000) ≈ 0.30 MJ/m³.
- Toughness (in a tensile test) = the area under the whole stress–strain curve.

Worked example
A steel bar (S275, E = 210 GPa), 20 mm in diameter and 2 m long, carries 60 kN in tension.
- A = π × 20²/4 = 314.2 mm², σ = 60 000/314.2 = 191 MPa (below 275 MPa, so elastic).
- ε = 191/210 000 = 9.09 × 10⁻⁴; extension = 9.09 × 10⁻⁴ × 2000 = 1.82 mm.
- With ν = 0.3, the diameter shrinks by 0.3 × 9.09 × 10⁻⁴ × 20 = 0.0055 mm.

Other tests
- Concrete compression: 150 mm cubes are common in UK practice; 150 × 300 mm cylinders are the basis of f_ck in Eurocode 2. Cubes give higher strengths because the platens restrain them more.
- Hardness (Brinell, Vickers, Rockwell): resistance to indentation, which correlates roughly with strength.
- Bending tests for timber; Charpy impact tests (next topic).

Characteristic values
Design codes use characteristic strengths, the value below which only 5% of results are expected to fall. For a normal distribution, f_k = f_mean − 1.64s. A concrete class such as C30/37 means a characteristic cylinder strength of 30 MPa and a characteristic cube strength of 37 MPa.

Exam tips: show units at every step (N and mm give MPa directly), check that the stress is below yield before using E, and label every feature on a sketched stress–strain curve.

Fracture
- Ductile fracture: extensive plastic deformation, necking, voids that grow and join, a "cup-and-cone" surface, high energy absorbed and visible warning.
- Brittle fracture: little plastic deformation, a fast-running crack (often cleavage in metals), low energy and little warning.

Griffith (1921) explained why brittle solids break far below their theoretical strength: small cracks concentrate stress. Linear elastic fracture mechanics expresses this through the stress intensity factor
K = Yσ√(πa)
where a is the crack length (the depth of an edge crack, or half the length of an internal crack) and Y is a geometry factor (about 1.12 for a small edge crack in a wide plate, 1.0 for a central crack in a wide plate). Fast fracture occurs when K reaches the fracture toughness K_IC (MPa√m).
Approximate K_IC values: structural steels from tens to over 100 MPa√m; aluminium alloys roughly 20–45; window glass about 0.7–0.8; concrete around 1 or less.
Worked example: a steel plate with K_IC = 50 MPa√m has a 5 mm edge crack (Y = 1.12). σ_f = 50/(1.12 × √(π × 0.005)) = 356 MPa. Rearranged, the critical crack length is a_c = (1/π)(K_IC/(Yσ))².
Holes and notches also concentrate stress: a circular hole in a wide plate under tension has a stress concentration factor of 3.

Impact and the ductile-to-brittle transition
The Charpy test strikes a notched bar with a pendulum and records the energy absorbed (J). Ferritic (BCC) steels show a ductile-to-brittle transition: tough at higher temperatures, brittle when cold. FCC metals (aluminium, copper, austenitic stainless steel) do not show a sharp transition. Brittle fractures of welded Liberty ships in the Second World War made this famous. Structural steel grades specify toughness, for example S355J2 requires 27 J at −20 °C (EN 10025).

Creep
Creep is time-dependent strain under constant stress.
- In metals it becomes significant above roughly 0.3–0.4 of the absolute melting temperature (the homologous temperature T/T_m). Lead at 20 °C has T/T_m ≈ 293/601 ≈ 0.49 and creeps noticeably; steel has T/T_m ≈ 0.16, so creep is negligible at room temperature but matters in fires.
- Concrete, timber and polymers creep at normal temperatures, so long-term deflections of beams and slabs grow for years.
- A creep curve has primary (decreasing rate), secondary (steady, minimum rate, used in design) and tertiary (accelerating to rupture) stages.
- Relaxation is the related loss of stress at constant strain, important in prestressing tendons.

Fatigue
Fatigue is failure under repeated loading at stresses below the static strength. It has three stages: crack initiation at a stress concentration (weld toe, hole, surface defect), stable crack growth (beach marks or striations on the fracture surface), and final fast fracture.
- The S–N (Wöhler) curve plots stress range against cycles to failure on log scales. Many steels show an endurance limit under constant amplitude loading; aluminium alloys do not.
- Welded steel details are designed with S–N curves in EN 1993-1-9.
- Miner's rule for variable loading: failure is predicted when Σ nᵢ/Nᵢ = 1.
Worked example: N = 10⁶ cycles at 200 MPa and 2 × 10⁵ at 300 MPa. After 4 × 10⁵ cycles at 200 MPa and 5 × 10⁴ at 300 MPa, damage = 0.4 + 0.25 = 0.65. Remaining life at 300 MPa = 0.35 × 2 × 10⁵ = 70 000 cycles.

Exam tips: always convert crack lengths to metres when K is in MPa√m, state the stage of a creep curve you are using, and remember that Miner's rule ignores the order in which loads are applied.

notes.h: Bonding and structure: metals, polymers and ceramics compared
notes.body:
Bonding explains much of a material's behaviour.
- Metallic bonding (delocalised electrons): ductile, tough, conducts heat and electricity.
- Ionic and covalent bonding (strong and directional): ceramics, which are stiff, hard, have high melting points and are brittle.
- Polymers: strong covalent bonds along long chains, but weak secondary bonds (van der Waals, hydrogen) between chains. This gives low stiffness, low melting or softening temperatures and creep.

Metals
Metals are crystalline. The common unit cells are:
- Body-centred cubic (BCC): ferritic iron at room temperature. 2 atoms per cell, atomic packing factor 0.68, coordination number 8.
- Face-centred cubic (FCC): aluminium, copper, nickel, and iron between about 912 °C and 1394 °C (austenite). 4 atoms per cell, packing factor 0.74, coordination number 12.
- Hexagonal close-packed (HCP): zinc, titanium, magnesium. Packing factor 0.74.
Real metals are polycrystals made of grains. Plastic deformation happens by dislocations moving on slip planes, which is why metals yield far below their theoretical strength. Ways of strengthening a metal (by obstructing dislocations) are solid-solution alloying, work hardening, grain refinement (Hall–Petch: σ_y = σ₀ + k d^(−1/2)), precipitation hardening, and heat treatment such as quenching and tempering.

Steel
Steel is iron with up to about 2 wt% carbon; above that the alloy is cast iron. Structural steels are low-carbon (roughly 0.25% or less) for ductility and weldability. Slowly cooled, they consist of ferrite plus pearlite, which is fine layers of ferrite and cementite (Fe₃C) formed at the eutectoid point (about 0.76–0.8% C, 727 °C). More carbon gives a harder, stronger, less ductile and less weldable steel. Stainless steels contain at least about 10.5% chromium.

Polymers
- Thermoplastics (polyethylene, PVC, polypropylene): linear or branched chains that soften on heating and can be remoulded. Used for pipes, membranes and geosynthetics.
- Thermosets (epoxy and polyester resins): chains cross-linked into a 3D network. They do not melt and char instead.
- Elastomers (rubber bearings): lightly cross-linked and used above their glass transition temperature.
- The glass transition temperature T_g separates a stiff, glassy state (below) from a rubbery state (above).
Polymers are viscoelastic, so their stiffness depends on time and temperature. Fibre-reinforced polymers (glass or carbon fibres in a resin) are used to strengthen existing structures.

Ceramics
Brick, stone, glass, cement paste and concrete (a ceramic composite) are stiff and strong in compression but weak and brittle in tension. Dislocations can hardly move, so small flaws act as Griffith cracks and fracture toughness is low.
In concrete, Portland cement hydrates (mainly C₃S and C₂S) to form calcium silicate hydrate (C–S–H) gel and calcium hydroxide, which bind aggregates making up roughly 60–75% of the volume. Strength falls as the water/cement ratio rises (Abrams, 1918). Tensile strength is only about a tenth of compressive strength, so steel reinforcement carries the tension in reinforced concrete.

Approximate property comparison (Eurocode values where stated)
- Structural steel S355: density 7850 kg/m³, E = 210 GPa, f_y = 355 MPa nominal for thinner sections.
- Reinforcing steel (B500 in the UK): f_yk = 500 MPa, E_s = 200 GPa.
- Concrete C30/37: density about 2400 kg/m³, f_ck = 30 MPa, f_ctm ≈ 2.9 MPa, E_cm ≈ 33 GPa (EN 1992-1-1).
- Aluminium alloy: density 2700 kg/m³, E ≈ 70 GPa.
- Softwood C24: mean density 420 kg/m³, E₀,mean = 11 GPa, f_m,k = 24 MPa (EN 338).
- Common polymers: density about 900–1400 kg/m³, E roughly 0.2–4 GPa.
A useful observation: the specific stiffness E/ρ is about 26 MJ/kg for steel, aluminium and timber along the grain, but only about 14 MJ/kg for concrete.

Exam tips: link each property back to bonding and microstructure, and quote approximate values with units and the word "approximately".

notes.h: Timber: structure, moisture, strength and durability
notes.body:
Softwoods and hardwoods
Softwoods come from conifers (gymnosperms such as spruce, pine, Douglas fir and larch). Hardwoods come from broadleaved trees (angiosperms such as oak, beech and ash). The names are botanical, not a measure of hardness: balsa is a hardwood. Most UK structural timber is softwood.

Structure
- Softwoods are mostly tracheids, long cells that both conduct water and give support. Hardwoods have vessels (pores) for conduction and fibres for strength.
- Each growth ring has earlywood (thin-walled, less dense) and latewood (thick-walled, denser).
- Sapwood is the outer, conducting wood. Heartwood is the inner, inactive wood, often containing extractives that make it more durable.
- Timber has three principal directions (longitudinal, radial and tangential) and different properties in each: it is orthotropic.

Chemical composition (approximate, by dry mass)
- Cellulose, about 40–50%: long-chain molecules forming crystalline microfibrils that give tensile strength.
- Hemicelluloses, about 20–35%.
- Lignin, about 15–35% (generally higher in softwoods): it binds and stiffens the cell wall.
- Small amounts of extractives.

Moisture
Moisture content (dry basis): MC = (m_wet − m_dry)/m_dry × 100%. It can exceed 100% in green timber.
Example: a sample of 52 g dries to 44 g in an oven, so MC = 8/44 = 18.2%.
- Free water sits in the cell cavities; bound water is held in the cell walls.
- The fibre saturation point (FSP) is about 25–30% MC. Below FSP, timber shrinks as it dries and gains strength and stiffness.
- Tangential shrinkage is roughly twice radial shrinkage; longitudinal shrinkage is very small. Uneven shrinkage causes cupping, twisting and splits.
- Eurocode 5 service classes: class 1 corresponds to most softwoods at no more than about 12% MC (heated interiors), class 2 to no more than about 20% (covered but unheated), and class 3 to wetter conditions.

Mechanical behaviour
- Timber is strongest and stiffest along the grain. E perpendicular to the grain is roughly a thirtieth of E parallel (C24: 0.37 GPa against 11 GPa).
- Tension perpendicular to the grain is very weak and causes splitting.
- Knots, slope of grain and fissures reduce strength, so structural timber is strength graded (visually or by machine) and assigned a class in EN 338: C classes for softwoods and D classes for hardwoods.
- EN 338 strengths are characteristic (5th percentile) values; stiffness is given as a mean. C24 has f_m,k = 24 MPa, f_c,0,k = 21 MPa, E₀,mean = 11 GPa and ρ_k = 350 kg/m³. C16 has f_m,k = 16 MPa, E₀,mean = 8 GPa and ρ_k = 310 kg/m³.
- Load duration and moisture matter. Timber is weaker under long-term load and creeps more when wet. Eurocode 5 uses k_mod for strength (for example 0.8 for solid timber under medium-term load in service class 1 or 2) and k_def for creep (0.6, 0.8 and 2.0 for solid timber in service classes 1, 2 and 3). The design strength is f_d = k_mod f_k/γ_M with γ_M = 1.3 for solid timber, so C24 in bending under medium-term load gives 0.8 × 24/1.3 = 14.8 MPa.

Durability
- Fungal decay (wet rots, and dry rot, Serpula lacrymans) needs moisture, roughly above 20% MC, plus oxygen and a suitable temperature.
- Insects such as the common furniture beetle attack timber, and marine borers attack it in sea water.
- Fire: timber chars at a fairly predictable rate (about 0.65 mm/min one-dimensionally for softwood, EN 1995-1-2). The char layer insulates the core, so large sections keep much of their strength.
- UV weathering greys the surface but is shallow.

Protection
- Protection by design: keep MC below about 20% by shedding water, ventilating, avoiding exposed end grain and using damp-proof courses.
- Choose naturally durable heartwood (EN 350 durability classes run from 1, very durable, to 5, not durable).
- Use preservative treatment matched to the EN 335 use class (UC1 interior dry up to UC4 ground or fresh-water contact and UC5 sea water).
- Use modified timber.

Exam tips: use the dry-basis MC formula, explain properties by direction (parallel or perpendicular to the grain), and link durability measures to keeping timber dry.

cards.b: A substance that deforms continuously under any shear stress, however small. So a fluid at rest carries no shear stress, only pressure.
A body force acts on the whole mass (gravity, ρg per unit volume). Surface forces act on the boundary: pressure (normal) and viscous shear (tangential).
τ = μ du/dy: shear stress equals dynamic viscosity × velocity gradient normal to the flow (for a Newtonian fluid).
ν = μ/ρ, units m²/s. Water at 20 °C: approximately 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s (μ ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa s).
Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν, the ratio of inertial to viscous forces. Guide values: laminar below about 2000, turbulent above about 4000.
Steady: conditions at a point don't change with time. Uniform: conditions don't change with position along the flow at a given instant.
Fluid in contact with a solid surface moves with that surface, so velocity gradients and shear stress are largest at the wall.
Absolute pressure = gauge pressure + atmospheric pressure (about 101.3 kPa at sea level). Gauge pressure is measured relative to the atmosphere.
Q = A₁V₁ = A₂V₂: the volume flow rate is the same at every section.
ṁ = ρAV (kg/s). For compressible steady flow ρ₁A₁V₁ = ρ₂A₂V₂.

cards.f: Velocity ratio in a circular pipe
cards.b: V₂/V₁ = (D₁/D₂)². Halving the diameter quadruples the velocity.
ΣQ in = ΣQ out (for steady incompressible flow, nothing is stored at the node).
A_tank dh/dt = Q_in − Q_out: the net inflow becomes storage, raising the level.
V = Q/A, the uniform velocity that would give the actual discharge. The real profile is zero at the wall and highest near the centre.
p = p₀ + ρgh. Pressure depends only on depth, not on the container's shape.
h = p/(ρg): the height of fluid column that produces pressure p.

cards.f: Resultant force on a plane surface
cards.b: F = ρg h_c A, where h_c is the depth of the centroid of area A.
y_p = y_c + I_G/(y_c A), with y measured along the plane from the free surface. It is always below the centroid.
Horizontal = force on the vertical projection. Vertical = weight of fluid (real or imaginary) between the surface and the free surface.
Upthrust = weight of fluid displaced, acting through the centroid of the displaced volume (the centre of buoyancy).
GM = BM − BG, with BM = I/V (waterplane second moment ÷ displaced volume). Stable if M lies above G (GM > 0).
Add ρgh going down, subtract going up; points at the same level in the same continuous fluid have equal pressure.
p/(ρg) + V²/(2g) + z = constant along a streamline.
Steady, incompressible, inviscid (no losses) flow along a streamline, with no pump or turbine work and no heat transfer.
p/(ρg) + z: the level to which water would rise in a piezometer. It is the HGL height.
Ideal jet speed from an orifice at depth h below a large tank's surface: V = √(2gh).
C_d = actual Q / ideal Q = C_c × C_v. Roughly 0.6 for a sharp-edged orifice; close to 1 for a Venturi meter.
Measures stagnation pressure p₀ = p + ½ρV², so V = √(2(p₀ − p)/ρ).
Q = C_d A₂ √(2gΔh/(1 − (A₂/A₁)²)), where Δh is the piezometric head difference between inlet and throat.
Head difference in metres of water = x(13.6 − 1) = 12.6x.
p₁/ρg + V₁²/2g + z₁ + h_p = p₂/ρg + V₂²/2g + z₂ + h_t + h_L.
h_f = f (L/D) V²/(2g), with f the Darcy friction factor (λ in many UK texts).
f = 64/Re (Darcy), equivalent to Hagen–Poiseuille Δp = 32μLV/D².
1/√f = −2 log₁₀(k_s/(3.7D) + 2.51/(Re√f)). Implicit in f: iterate or use the Moody diagram.
K = 1.0: the whole velocity head V²/(2g) is lost.
EGL = p/ρg + V²/2g + z. HGL = p/ρg + z, one velocity head below the EGL. Pressure is sub-atmospheric where the HGL is below the pipe.
P = ρgQH_p/η, where H_p is the head the pump adds and η the pump efficiency.
Series: same Q, losses add. Parallel: same head loss in each branch, flows add.
σ = Eε within the elastic (linear) range.
ν = −lateral strain/axial strain. Approximately 0.3 for steel and 0.2 for concrete.
The stress where a line parallel to the elastic slope, offset by 0.2% strain, meets the stress–strain curve. Used when there is no clear yield point.
The maximum engineering stress in a tensile test (maximum load ÷ original area). Necking begins there.
Percentage elongation after fracture and percentage reduction of area at fracture.
Elastic strain energy per unit volume up to yield = σ_y²/(2E). About 0.30 MJ/m³ for S355 with E = 210 GPa.
The 5% fractile: only 5% of results are expected to be lower. For a normal distribution f_k = f_mean − 1.64s.
Characteristic cylinder strength f_ck = 30 MPa; characteristic cube strength 37 MPa (Eurocode 2 / EN 206).
K = Yσ√(πa). Fast fracture when K reaches the fracture toughness K_IC (MPa√m).
Ductile: large plastic strain, necking, high energy, warning. Brittle: little plastic strain, fast crack, low energy, little warning.
A pendulum breaks a notched bar; the energy absorbed (J) measures toughness at the test temperature.
BCC (ferritic) steels become brittle below a transition temperature. FCC metals such as aluminium show no sharp transition.
Primary (decreasing rate), secondary (steady minimum rate), tertiary (accelerating to rupture).
T/T_m in kelvin. Creep in metals is significant above about 0.3–0.4. Lead at 20 °C is about 0.49; steel about 0.16.
Failure is predicted when Σ nᵢ/Nᵢ = 1. It assumes linear damage accumulation and ignores load sequence.
Initiation at a stress concentration, stable growth (beach marks or striations), then final fast fracture.
BCC: 2 atoms per cell, packing factor 0.68 (ferritic iron). FCC: 4 atoms per cell, packing factor 0.74 (aluminium, copper, austenite).

cards.f: Why metals yield below theoretical strength
cards.b: Plastic deformation happens by dislocation movement, which needs far less stress than shearing whole planes of atoms at once.
σ_y = σ₀ + k d^(−1/2): finer grains give a higher yield strength.
Steel: iron with up to about 2 wt% carbon (structural steels about 0.25% or less). Cast iron: more than about 2% carbon.
Thermoplastics soften on heating and can be remoulded (PE, PVC). Thermosets are cross-linked networks that do not melt (epoxy).
T_g: below it a polymer is glassy and stiff; above it, rubbery and much less stiff.
Strong directional bonds prevent dislocation movement, so small flaws act as Griffith cracks and fracture toughness is low.
f_ck = 30 MPa, f_cm = 38 MPa, f_ctm ≈ 2.9 MPa, E_cm ≈ 33 GPa (approximate tabulated values).
Botanical: softwoods are conifers (gymnosperms); hardwoods are broadleaved trees (angiosperms). Balsa is a hardwood.
MC = (m_wet − m_dry)/m_dry × 100%. It can exceed 100% in green timber.
About 25–30% MC. Below it, cell walls lose bound water: timber shrinks and its strength and stiffness rise.
Cellulose (about 40–50%), hemicelluloses (about 20–35%) and lignin (about 15–35%), plus extractives. Approximate dry-mass shares.
f_m,k = 24 MPa, f_c,0,k = 21 MPa, E₀,mean = 11 GPa, ρ_k = 350 kg/m³.
Moisture content above roughly 20%, oxygen and a suitable temperature. Keeping timber dry prevents decay.
UC1 interior dry; UC2 occasional wetting; UC3 exterior above ground; UC4 ground or fresh-water contact; UC5 sea water.
Modifies strength for load duration and moisture: f_d = k_mod f_k/γ_M (γ_M = 1.3 for solid timber).

questions.q: A flat plate of area 0.5 m² slides at 0.5 m/s over a 2 mm thick film of oil (μ = 0.08 Pa s) on a fixed surface. Assuming a linear velocity profile, what force is needed to keep the plate moving?
questions.why: τ = μU/h = 0.08 × 0.5/0.002 = 20 Pa, and F = τA = 20 × 0.5 = 10 N. The 20 N answer is the shear stress in pascals, never multiplied by the area. The 0.01 N answer comes from leaving the film thickness in millimetres (h = 2). The 40 N answer comes from dividing the stress by the area instead of multiplying.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a fluid from a solid?
options: A fluid always has a lower density than a solid.
A fluid deforms continuously under any shear stress, however small, so a fluid at rest carries no shear stress.
A fluid has zero viscosity when it is at rest.
A fluid offers no resistance to compression.
questions.why: The defining property of a fluid is that it cannot resist shear at rest: any shear stress produces continuous deformation. Saying fluids offer no resistance to compression is wrong, because liquids are nearly incompressible (water's bulk modulus is about 2.2 GPa). The density claim is wrong because mercury (about 13 600 kg/m³) is denser than steel (about 7850 kg/m³). Viscosity is a material property that does not vanish at rest; the shear stress in a static fluid is zero because the velocity gradient is zero.

questions.q: (a) Distinguish between steady and uniform flow. (b) Water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, μ = 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa s) flows at a mean velocity of 0.03 m/s in a 50 mm diameter pipe. Calculate the Reynolds number and state the likely flow regime. (c) At what mean velocity would Re reach 4000?
markScheme: Steady: no change with time at a point; uniform: no change with position along the flow (1 mark each)
Laminar, since Re is below about 2000 (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Steady flow means that the velocity, pressure and other properties at any fixed point do not change with time. Uniform flow means that, at a given instant, they are the same at every position along the flow. A constant discharge through a tapering pipe is steady but non-uniform.
(b) Re = ρVD/μ = 1000 × 0.03 × 0.05/(1.0 × 10⁻³) = 1500. This is below the usual guide value of about 2000, so the flow is expected to be laminar.
(c) Rearranging, V = Re μ/(ρD) = 4000 × 1.0 × 10⁻³/(1000 × 0.05) = 0.08 m/s. Above roughly this velocity the flow would be expected to be fully turbulent.

questions.q: A pipe carrying water reduces from 300 mm to 150 mm diameter. The mean velocity in the 300 mm section is 1.2 m/s. What is the mean velocity in the 150 mm section?
questions.why: Continuity gives V₂ = V₁(A₁/A₂) = V₁(D₁/D₂)² = 1.2 × 2² = 4.8 m/s. The 2.4 m/s answer scales by the diameter ratio instead of the area ratio. The 0.3 m/s answer uses the squared ratio upside down (dividing by 4), and the 0.6 m/s answer uses the unsquared ratio upside down (dividing by 2). The smaller pipe must carry the same discharge at a higher velocity.

questions.q: A water main carrying 0.10 m³/s divides into two branches. Branch 2 has a diameter of 200 mm and a mean velocity of 2.0 m/s. What is the discharge in branch 3?
questions.why: Q₂ = (π/4)(0.2)²(2.0) = 0.0628 m³/s, so Q₃ = 0.10 − 0.0628 = 0.037 m³/s. The 0.084 m³/s answer comes from putting the radius (0.1 m) into πD²/4, which underestimates Q₂ as 0.0157 m³/s. The 0.020 m³/s answer treats the pipe area as D² (a square section), giving Q₂ = 0.08 m³/s. The 0.063 m³/s answer is the flow in branch 2, not branch 3.

questions.q: A rectangular channel 4 m wide carries water 1.5 m deep at a mean velocity of 0.8 m/s. Downstream it narrows to 3 m wide, where the depth is 1.2 m. Find the discharge and the mean velocity in the narrow section, and state the assumption you make.
markScheme: Downstream area = 3 × 1.2 = 3.6 m² (1 mark)
Assumption: steady flow of an incompressible fluid with no inflow or outflow between the sections (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: Assuming steady, incompressible flow with no lateral inflow or losses of water between the two sections, the discharge is constant. Upstream, A₁ = 4 × 1.5 = 6.0 m², so Q = A₁V₁ = 6.0 × 0.8 = 4.8 m³/s. Downstream, A₂ = 3 × 1.2 = 3.6 m², so V₂ = Q/A₂ = 4.8/3.6 = 1.33 m/s. The velocity increases because the flow area is smaller.

questions.q: A vertical rectangular gate 2 m wide and 3 m high has its top edge 1 m below the water surface. What is the resultant hydrostatic force on the gate? (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²)
questions.why: F = ρg h_c A with the centroid at h_c = 1 + 1.5 = 2.5 m and A = 6 m², so F = 1000 × 9.81 × 2.5 × 6 = 147 kN. The 58.9 kN answer uses the depth of the top edge (1 m) and the 235 kN answer the depth of the bottom edge (4 m). The 165 kN answer uses the depth of the centre of pressure (2.8 m); the centre of pressure tells you where the force acts, but its magnitude depends on the centroid depth.

questions.q: A water pipe is connected to a U-tube manometer containing mercury (ρ = 13 600 kg/m³), open to the atmosphere. The mercury in the open limb stands 0.25 m above the mercury surface in the limb connected to the pipe, and the pipe centre is 0.10 m above that lower mercury surface. What is the gauge pressure at the pipe centre?
questions.why: Equal pressures at the level of the lower mercury surface give p_A + 1000g(0.10) = 13 600g(0.25), so p_A = 33.35 − 0.98 = 32.4 kPa. The 34.3 kPa answer adds the 0.10 m water column instead of subtracting it: the pipe is above the interface, so its pressure is lower. The 33.4 kPa answer ignores the water column altogether. The 1.47 kPa answer uses the density of water for the manometer fluid.

questions.q: A vertical rectangular gate 1.5 m wide and 2 m high is hinged along its top edge, which is 0.5 m below the water surface. Water acts on one side only. Find (a) the resultant hydrostatic force, (b) the depth of the centre of pressure, and (c) the horizontal force needed at the bottom edge to keep the gate closed.
markScheme: y_p = 1.5 + 1.0/(1.5 × 3) = 1.72 m below the surface (1 mark)
Moment about the hinge: 44.15 × (1.722 − 0.5) ≈ 54.0 kN m (1 mark)
Force at the bottom edge = 54.0/2 = 27.0 kN (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The centroid is at depth h_c = 0.5 + 1.0 = 1.5 m and A = 1.5 × 2 = 3 m². F = ρg h_c A = 1000 × 9.81 × 1.5 × 3 = 44 145 N ≈ 44.1 kN.
(b) I_G = bd³/12 = 1.5 × 2³/12 = 1.0 m⁴. y_p = y_c + I_G/(y_c A) = 1.5 + 1.0/(1.5 × 3) = 1.722 m below the surface.
(c) The hinge is at 0.5 m depth, so the lever arm of F about the hinge is 1.722 − 0.5 = 1.222 m and the moment is 44.145 × 1.222 = 53.96 kN m. The restraining force P acts at the bottom edge, 2 m from the hinge: P × 2 = 53.96, giving P ≈ 27.0 kN.

questions.q: A horizontal Venturi meter has an inlet diameter of 200 mm and a throat diameter of 100 mm and carries water. A mercury–water differential manometer (mercury relative density 13.6) between inlet and throat shows a reading of 0.2 m. What is the ideal (C_d = 1) discharge?
questions.why: The head difference in metres of water is Δh = 0.2 × (13.6 − 1) = 2.52 m. Then Q = A₂√(2gΔh/(1 − (A₂/A₁)²)) = 7.854 × 10⁻³ × √(2 × 9.81 × 2.52/(1 − 1/16)) = 0.0570 m³/s. The 0.0161 m³/s answer treats the 0.2 m reading as metres of water. The 0.0593 m³/s answer converts with 13.6 instead of (13.6 − 1), ignoring the water above the mercury in both limbs. The 0.0552 m³/s answer leaves out the velocity of approach factor 1 − (A₂/A₁)².

questions.q: Which set of conditions must hold for p/(ρg) + V²/(2g) + z to be constant?
options: Steady, incompressible, inviscid flow along a streamline, with no pump or turbine work
Laminar flow of any fluid, compressible or not, between any two points
Uniform flow in a pipe, including the effect of wall friction
Unsteady flow, provided the fluid is incompressible
questions.why: Bernoulli's equation comes from Newton's second law along a streamline for steady, frictionless, incompressible flow with no shaft work. Laminar flow of a compressible fluid is wrong on two counts: compressibility invalidates the constant-density form, and laminar flow still has viscous losses. Including wall friction contradicts the inviscid assumption; friction is handled by adding a head loss in the energy equation. Unsteady flow needs an extra ∂V/∂t term, so incompressibility alone is not enough.

questions.q: Water discharges to atmosphere through a sharp-edged orifice of diameter 25 mm in the side of a large tank. The orifice is 5 m below the water surface, which is held constant. (a) Find the ideal jet velocity. (b) Find the actual discharge if C_d = 0.62. (c) Explain why C_d is less than 1.
markScheme: Bernoulli from the free surface (p = 0, V ≈ 0, z = 5) to the jet (p = 0): V = √(2gh) (1 mark)
Actual Q = 0.62 × 4.86 × 10⁻³ = 3.01 × 10⁻³ m³/s (about 3.0 L/s) (1 mark)
C_d = C_c × C_v: the jet contracts to a vena contracta and friction makes the velocity slightly less than ideal (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Apply Bernoulli between the free surface (gauge pressure 0, velocity negligible in a large tank, elevation 5 m above the orifice) and the jet just outside the orifice (gauge pressure 0, elevation 0): 5 = V²/(2g), so V = √(2 × 9.81 × 5) = 9.90 m/s.
(b) Orifice area a = π × 0.025²/4 = 4.91 × 10⁻⁴ m². Ideal Q = aV = 4.86 × 10⁻³ m³/s. Actual Q = C_d × ideal Q = 0.62 × 4.86 × 10⁻³ = 3.01 × 10⁻³ m³/s, about 3.0 L/s.
(c) C_d = C_c × C_v. Streamlines cannot turn sharply at the edge of the orifice, so the jet keeps contracting to a minimum area (the vena contracta), and C_c is typically about 0.6 or more. Viscous effects also make the real velocity slightly below √(2gh), so C_v is just under 1. Together these give C_d of roughly 0.6.

questions.q: Water flows at 1.5 m/s through a 200 mm diameter pipe, 500 m long. The Darcy friction factor is f = 0.02. What is the friction head loss?
questions.why: Darcy–Weisbach gives h_f = f(L/D)V²/(2g) = 0.02 × (500/0.2) × 1.5²/19.62 = 5.73 m. The 22.9 m answer uses the Fanning form h_f = 4fLV²/(2gD) with a Darcy factor, which is four times too large. The 112.5 m answer omits the 2g in the velocity head. The 11.5 m answer uses the radius (0.1 m) instead of the diameter.

questions.q: Oil (ρ = 900 kg/m³, μ = 0.1 Pa s) flows at a mean velocity of 1.0 m/s through a 50 mm diameter pipe, 20 m long. What is the friction head loss, in metres of oil?
questions.why: Re = ρVD/μ = 900 × 1.0 × 0.05/0.1 = 450, so the flow is laminar and f = 64/Re = 0.142. Then h_f = 0.142 × (20/0.05) × 1.0²/19.62 = 2.90 m of oil (the same as Hagen–Poiseuille, Δp = 32μLV/D² = 25.6 kPa, divided by ρ_oil g). The 0.73 m answer uses 16/Re, the laminar Fanning factor, in the Darcy equation. The 2.61 m answer converts the 25.6 kPa pressure drop to head using the density of water instead of oil. The 5.80 m answer drops the factor of 2 in V²/(2g).

questions.q: A pump lifts water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³) at 0.05 m³/s from a sump to a tank whose free surface is 25 m higher. The total head loss in the pipework is 3.5 m. (a) Write the steady-flow energy equation between the two free surfaces and find the pump head. (b) Find the hydraulic power and the shaft power if the pump efficiency is 75%.
markScheme: SFEE between free surfaces: p and V terms vanish (atmospheric, large surfaces), so z₁ + h_p = z₂ + h_L (1 mark)
Hydraulic power = ρgQh_p = 1000 × 9.81 × 0.05 × 28.5 = 13.98 kW (1 mark)
Shaft power = 13.98/0.75 = 18.6 kW (1 mark)
Correct units and a clear statement of assumptions (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Between the sump surface (1) and the tank surface (2): p₁/ρg + V₁²/2g + z₁ + h_p = p₂/ρg + V₂²/2g + z₂ + h_L. Both surfaces are at atmospheric pressure (gauge 0) and, being large, have negligible velocity. So h_p = (z₂ − z₁) + h_L = 25 + 3.5 = 28.5 m.
(b) Hydraulic power = ρgQh_p = 1000 × 9.81 × 0.05 × 28.5 = 13 980 W ≈ 14.0 kW. The pump is 75% efficient, so the shaft power required is 13.98/0.75 = 18.6 kW.

questions.q: A 20 mm diameter S275 steel bar (E = 210 GPa), 2 m long, carries an axial tensile load of 60 kN. What is its extension?
options: It cannot be found using E because the bar has yielded
questions.why: A = π × 20²/4 = 314.2 mm², σ = 60 000/314.2 = 191 MPa, ε = 191/210 000 = 9.09 × 10⁻⁴, and the extension is 9.09 × 10⁻⁴ × 2000 = 1.82 mm. The 0.455 mm answer uses πd² for the area, leaving out the divide-by-4. The 7.28 mm answer puts the radius (10 mm) into πd²/4. The bar has not yielded, because 191 MPa is well below the 275 MPa nominal yield strength, so Hooke's law applies.

questions.q: How is the 0.2% proof stress of a metal defined?
options: The stress at which the total strain reaches 0.2%
The stress where a line parallel to the initial elastic slope, offset by 0.2% strain, meets the stress–strain curve
The stress at which the cross-sectional area has fallen by 0.2%
questions.why: Proof stress uses an offset line: a 0.2% permanent (plastic) strain. Reading the stress at 0.2% total strain is wrong because the total includes the elastic strain; for a steel yielding near 355 MPa the elastic strain alone is about 0.17%. Taking 0.2% of the UTS confuses a strain offset with a fraction of stress. A 0.2% reduction in area is a necking or ductility measure, not the definition of proof stress.

questions.q: Tests on 150 mm concrete cubes give a mean strength of 45 MPa with a standard deviation of 4.5 MPa. (a) Explain what is meant by characteristic strength. (b) Estimate the characteristic cube strength, assuming a normal distribution. (c) Explain why cube strengths are higher than cylinder strengths for the same concrete.
markScheme: Characteristic strength is the 5% fractile: only 5% of results are expected to fall below it (1 mark)
f_k = f_mean − 1.64s (1 mark)
Friction at the platens restrains lateral expansion; this restraint affects more of a squat cube than a 2:1 cylinder (1 mark)
so cubes show higher strength (e.g. C30/37: cylinder 30 MPa, cube 37 MPa) (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Strength varies from batch to batch and specimen to specimen. The characteristic strength is the value below which only 5% of all results are expected to fall (the 5% fractile). Designers use it so that the strength assumed in design is very likely to be achieved.
(b) For a normal distribution the 5% fractile lies 1.64 standard deviations below the mean: f_k = 45 − 1.64 × 4.5 = 37.6 MPa (cube). On this simple basis it just reaches the 37 MPa characteristic cube strength of class C30/37.
(c) In a compression test, friction between the steel platens and the specimen restrains the specimen's lateral expansion near its ends, creating confinement that raises the failure load. A cube (height equal to width) is restrained over most of its height, whereas the central part of a 2:1 cylinder is relatively free. Cubes therefore give higher strengths, which is why classes are written as cylinder/cube, e.g. C30/37.

questions.q: A steel plate (K_IC = 50 MPa√m) contains an edge crack 5 mm deep. Taking Y = 1.12, what tensile stress will cause fast fracture?
questions.why: σ_f = K_IC/(Y√(πa)) = 50/(1.12 × √(π × 0.005)) = 356 MPa. The 11.3 MPa answer puts the crack length in millimetres (a = 5), which is inconsistent with units of MPa√m. The 631 MPa answer leaves π out of the square root. The 504 MPa answer halves the crack length to 2.5 mm, as if 5 mm were the full length 2a of an internal crack; for an edge crack, a is the whole depth.

questions.q: A component has fatigue lives of 1 × 10⁶ cycles at a stress range of 200 MPa and 2 × 10⁵ cycles at 300 MPa. It has already seen 4 × 10⁵ cycles at 200 MPa and 5 × 10⁴ cycles at 300 MPa. Using Miner's rule, how many more cycles at 300 MPa can it take?
questions.why: The damage so far is 4 × 10⁵/10⁶ + 5 × 10⁴/(2 × 10⁵) = 0.40 + 0.25 = 0.65, so the remaining fraction 0.35 × 2 × 10⁵ = 70 000 cycles at 300 MPa. The 350 000 answer multiplies the remaining fraction by the 200 MPa life instead of the 300 MPa life. The 130 000 answer uses the damage already used (0.65) instead of the damage remaining. The 150 000 answer subtracts only the 300 MPa cycles from N₂, ignoring the damage done at 200 MPa.

questions.q: (a) Sketch and describe the three stages of a typical creep curve. (b) Explain, using the homologous temperature, why a lead roof sheet creeps at room temperature but a steel beam does not (T_m: lead 327.5 °C, iron 1538 °C). (c) Give one consequence of creep in concrete structures.
markScheme: Primary: strain rate decreasing; secondary: steady, minimum rate; tertiary: accelerating rate to rupture (sketch of strain against time) (2 marks)
Lead: 293/601 ≈ 0.49, above the threshold of about 0.3–0.4, so creep is significant (1 mark)
Steel: 293/1811 ≈ 0.16, well below the threshold, so creep is negligible at room temperature (1 mark)
Concrete: long-term deflections increase, or prestress is lost over time (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Plotting strain against time at constant stress: after the instantaneous elastic strain, primary creep has a decreasing strain rate as the material work-hardens. Secondary (steady-state) creep has a constant, minimum strain rate, the stage used in design. Tertiary creep has an accelerating strain rate as necking, voids and cracks develop, ending in rupture.
(b) Creep in metals depends on the homologous temperature T/T_m in kelvin and becomes important above about 0.3–0.4. At 20 °C (293 K), lead has T/T_m = 293/600.7 ≈ 0.49, so atoms are mobile enough for creep, and lead sheet slowly sags and thins on roofs. Iron has T_m ≈ 1811 K, so T/T_m ≈ 0.16 and creep is negligible at room temperature (though it becomes important in a fire).
(c) Concrete creeps at normal temperatures, so beams and slabs keep deflecting for years after loading, and prestressed members lose part of their prestress over time.

questions.q: Ferritic iron at room temperature is body-centred cubic (BCC). How many atoms belong to each unit cell, and what is its atomic packing factor?
questions.why: In BCC, the 8 corner atoms are each shared by 8 cells (contributing 1 atom) and there is 1 atom at the centre, so there are 2 atoms per cell and the packing factor is 0.68. 4 atoms and 0.74 describe FCC (aluminium, copper, austenite). 1 atom and 0.52 describe simple cubic. 9 atoms comes from counting every corner atom as whole instead of sharing it between 8 cells.

questions.q: Which statement about the approximate properties of construction materials is correct?
options: Polymers such as PVC are stiffer than concrete.
The tensile strength of concrete is roughly one-tenth of its compressive strength.
Ceramics are tough because their ionic and covalent bonds are strong.
Aluminium alloys have a higher Young's modulus than structural steel.
questions.why: For C30/37 concrete, f_ctm ≈ 2.9 MPa against f_ck = 30 MPa, about one-tenth, which is why concrete is reinforced. The aluminium claim is false: aluminium alloys have E ≈ 70 GPa against about 210 GPa for steel. The PVC claim is false: PVC has E of only a few GPa against about 33 GPa for C30/37 concrete. The ceramics claim confuses stiffness with toughness: strong directional bonds make ceramics stiff and hard, but they stop dislocations moving, so ceramics are brittle with low fracture toughness.

questions.q: Distinguish between thermoplastics, thermosets and elastomers in terms of molecular structure, giving one civil engineering use of each. What is the significance of the glass transition temperature?
markScheme: Thermoplastic: linear or branched chains held by weak secondary bonds; softens on heating and can be remoulded; e.g. HDPE or PVC pipes (1 mark)
Thermoset: densely cross-linked 3D network; does not melt; e.g. epoxy resin adhesives or FRP matrices (1 mark)
Elastomer: lightly cross-linked chains used above T_g; large recoverable strains; e.g. rubber bridge bearings (1 mark)
T_g: below it the polymer is glassy, stiff and brittle; above it, rubbery and much less stiff (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer:
Thermoplastics consist of long linear or branched chains held together by weak secondary bonds. Heating weakens these bonds, so the material softens and can be reshaped and recycled. Examples are HDPE and PVC water and drainage pipes.
Thermosets are cured into a densely cross-linked three-dimensional network of covalent bonds, so they do not melt on heating but eventually char. Epoxy resins used as structural adhesives and as the matrix of fibre-reinforced polymer strengthening plates are examples.
Elastomers are lightly cross-linked and used above their glass transition temperature, so the chains can uncoil and recoil, giving large recoverable strains. Rubber (elastomeric) bridge bearings are an example.
The glass transition temperature T_g marks the change from a glassy state, where chain segments cannot move and the polymer is stiff and brittle, to a rubbery state, where segments can rotate and stiffness drops sharply. A polymer's behaviour in service therefore depends on whether it is used above or below T_g.

questions.q: A timber sample weighs 52 g. After oven drying it weighs 44 g. What is its moisture content?
questions.why: Moisture content uses the oven-dry mass as the base: MC = (52 − 44)/44 × 100 = 18.2%. The 15.4% answer divides the water mass by the wet mass. The 84.6% answer is the dry mass as a percentage of the wet mass. The 118% answer is the wet mass as a percentage of the dry mass, without subtracting the dry mass.

questions.q: In Eurocode 5 the design strength is f_d = k_mod f_k/γ_M. For C24 timber in bending (f_m,k = 24 MPa) under medium-term load in service class 1, k_mod = 0.8 and γ_M = 1.3. What is the design bending strength?
questions.why: f_m,d = 0.8 × 24/1.3 = 14.8 MPa. The 19.2 MPa answer applies k_mod but forgets to divide by the material partial factor. The 18.5 MPa answer divides by γ_M but leaves out k_mod. The 25.0 MPa answer multiplies by γ_M instead of dividing, which would make the design strength larger than the characteristic strength.

questions.q: Explain what conditions allow fungal decay of timber in buildings, and describe three different ways a designer can ensure that external timber (e.g. cladding or a footbridge deck) is durable.
markScheme: Decay fungi need moisture content above roughly 20%, plus oxygen and a suitable temperature (1 mark)
Protection by design: shed water, ventilate, avoid water traps and exposed end grain, keep timber off the ground or masonry with DPCs, so MC stays below about 20% (1 mark)
Species selection: naturally durable heartwood (EN 350 durability classes 1–2); sapwood is not durable (1 mark)
Preservative treatment or modified timber matched to the EN 335 use class (e.g. UC3 for exterior above ground) (1 mark)
Maintenance and inspection (coatings, replacing sacrificial elements) or another valid measure, clearly explained (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer:
Wood-decaying fungi (wet rots, and dry rot, Serpula lacrymans) can only colonise timber that stays wet, roughly above 20% moisture content, with oxygen available and temperatures in a suitable range. Timber that stays dry, or permanently waterlogged with no oxygen, does not decay.
A designer can make external timber durable in several ways:
- Protection by design. Detail the timber so it sheds water and dries quickly: slope surfaces, leave ventilation gaps, avoid water traps and horizontal end grain, cap exposed ends, and keep timber off the ground and away from wet masonry using damp-proof courses. The aim is to keep the moisture content below about 20% for most of the time.
- Material selection. Specify the heartwood of a naturally durable species (EN 350 durability class 1 or 2, such as oak heartwood or larch heartwood for some uses). Sapwood of any species should be treated as non-durable.
- Treatment. Use preservative-treated or modified timber (e.g. acetylated or thermally modified) appropriate to the EN 335 use class: UC3 for cladding and decks above ground, UC4 for posts in ground contact.
Regular inspection and maintenance (re-coating, replacing sacrificial boards) further extends service life.

questions.q:
Two reservoirs are connected by a 300 mm diameter pipeline, 1200 m long. The water surface in reservoir A is at 50.0 m above datum and in reservoir B at 30.0 m. The Darcy friction factor is f = 0.018. Local loss coefficients are 0.5 at the entrance, 2.0 for a valve near the downstream end, and 1.0 at the exit. Take ρ = 1000 kg/m³, ν = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s, g = 9.81 m/s².
(a) Apply the steady-flow energy equation to find the mean velocity and the discharge. [8]
(b) The pipe passes over a high point C at elevation 51.0 m, 400 m from the entrance (upstream of the valve). Find the pressure at C as a gauge pressure and as an absolute pressure (p_atm = 101.3 kPa), and comment. [6]
(c) Calculate the Reynolds number. Using the Colebrook–White equation with k_s = 0.15 mm, check whether f = 0.018 is reasonable and estimate the effect on the discharge. [4]
(d) Sketch the energy and hydraulic grade lines along the pipeline. [2]
markScheme: (a) SFEE between free surfaces: z_A − z_B = (K_ent + K_valve + K_exit + fL/D)V²/(2g) (2 marks)
(a) fL/D = 0.018 × 1200/0.3 = 72; total coefficient = 75.5 (2 marks)
(b) Energy from A to C: 50 = p_C/ρg + 51 + (1 + 0.5 + 24)V²/(2g); p_C/ρg = −7.75 m (3 marks)

(b) p_C = −76.1 kPa gauge ≈ 25 kPa absolute; above vapour pressure (about 2.3 kPa), so no cavitation, but sub-atmospheric with a risk of air release and accumulation; reroute or lower the pipe (3 marks)
(c) Re = VD/ν ≈ 6.8 × 10⁵ (turbulent); Colebrook gives f ≈ 0.0174 (2 marks)
(c) f = 0.018 is slightly conservative; re-solving gives V ≈ 2.32 m/s, Q ≈ 0.164 m³/s (about 1.6% more) (2 marks)

(d) EGL starts at 50 m, drops at the entrance, falls linearly along the pipe, drops at the valve and exit to 30 m; HGL is one velocity head (0.265 m) below the EGL in the pipe and dips below the pipe at C (2 marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Apply the SFEE between the free surfaces of A and B. Both are at atmospheric pressure with negligible velocity, so the difference in level is used up entirely by losses:
z_A − z_B = (K_ent + K_valve + K_exit + fL/D) V²/(2g)
fL/D = 0.018 × 1200/0.3 = 72, so the total loss coefficient is 0.5 + 2.0 + 1.0 + 72 = 75.5.
20.0 = 75.5 V²/(2g), giving V²/(2g) = 0.2649 m and V = √(2 × 9.81 × 0.2649) = 2.28 m/s.
A = π × 0.3²/4 = 0.0707 m², so Q = 0.0707 × 2.28 = 0.161 m³/s (161 L/s).

(b) Apply the SFEE from the surface of A to point C, including the entrance loss and friction over 400 m (the valve is downstream of C):
50.0 = p_C/(ρg) + V²/(2g) + 51.0 + (0.5 + 0.018 × 400/0.3) V²/(2g)
0.018 × 400/0.3 = 24, so the velocity-head coefficient is 1 + 0.5 + 24 = 25.5.
p_C/(ρg) = 50.0 − 51.0 − 25.5 × 0.2649 = −1.0 − 6.755 = −7.75 m of water.
p_C = 1000 × 9.81 × (−7.755) = −76.1 kPa gauge, which is about 101.3 − 76.1 = 25.2 kPa absolute.
Comment: the pressure is well below atmospheric because C lies above the hydraulic grade line. It is still above the vapour pressure of water (about 2.3 kPa at 20 °C), so the water will not boil and the flow can continue (the pipe acts partly as a siphon). However, dissolved air will tend to come out of solution and collect at C, which can reduce the flow and, if the pressure falls further, lead to cavitation. Leaky joints there could also draw in contaminated groundwater. A designer would normally lower the pipe at C, or change the layout, so that it stays below the HGL.

(c) Re = VD/ν = 2.28 × 0.3/(1.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 6.84 × 10⁵, so the flow is fully turbulent.
Colebrook–White: 1/√f = −2 log₁₀(k_s/(3.7D) + 2.51/(Re√f)), with k_s/(3.7D) = 0.00015/1.11 = 1.35 × 10⁻⁴. Starting from f = 0.018: 2.51/(6.84 × 10⁵ × 0.134) = 2.74 × 10⁻⁵, the sum is 1.625 × 10⁻⁴, 1/√f = 7.58, so f = 0.0174. A further iteration changes it very little.
The given f = 0.018 is therefore slightly high (conservative). Re-solving with f ≈ 0.0174 gives fL/D = 69.7, a total coefficient of 73.2, V ≈ 2.32 m/s and Q ≈ 0.164 m³/s, about 1.6% more flow. The answer to (a) is reasonable for design.

(d) The EGL starts at 50.0 m at reservoir A, drops by 0.5V²/(2g) = 0.13 m at the entrance, and then falls linearly with friction (19.07 m over 1200 m). It drops by 2V²/(2g) = 0.53 m at the valve and by the exit loss of 0.26 m to finish at 30.0 m at reservoir B. In the pipe, the HGL runs parallel to the EGL and 0.265 m below it (starting at about 49.6 m just after the entrance). Because the exit loss equals one velocity head, the HGL at the pipe exit is at 30.0 m, level with the B water surface. At C the pipe (51 m) lies about 7.75 m above the HGL, which shows the sub-atmospheric pressure.

questions.q:
A tensile test is carried out on a steel specimen with an original diameter of 10.0 mm and a gauge length of 50.0 mm. At a load of 20.0 kN, still within the linear region, the extensometer reads an extension of 0.060 mm. The 0.2% proof load is 28.0 kN and the maximum load is 40.0 kN. After fracture, the gauge length is 61.0 mm and the minimum diameter at the neck is 6.5 mm.
(a) Determine Young's modulus, the 0.2% proof stress, the ultimate tensile strength, the percentage elongation and the percentage reduction of area. Comment on the ductility of the steel. [8]
(b) A wide plate of this steel, with fracture toughness K_IC = 60 MPa√m, is to operate at a tensile stress of 200 MPa. Taking Y = 1.12 for an edge crack, find the critical crack depth. [4]
(c) A welded detail in the same structure has an S–N relationship N = 1.024 × 10¹²/S³ (S = stress range in MPa). Each year it experiences 3 × 10⁴ cycles at a stress range of 100 MPa and 1.5 × 10⁵ cycles at 60 MPa. Use Miner's rule to estimate its fatigue life. [5]
(d) The structure is an exposed bridge in the UK. Explain why the steel would be specified with a Charpy impact grade such as J2. [3]
markScheme: (a) Proof stress = 28 000/78.54 = 357 MPa; UTS = 40 000/78.54 = 509 MPa (2 marks)
(a) Elongation = 11/50 = 22%; reduction of area = 1 − (6.5/10)² = 57.8%; a ductile steel (2 marks for values, 2 for comment and method) (4 marks)
(c) Comment on Miner's rule assumptions (linear damage, sequence ignored) (1 mark)

(d) Ferritic steel has a ductile-to-brittle transition; UK winter temperatures can be below zero; J2 guarantees 27 J at −20 °C, so the steel stays tough and cracks do not run in a brittle way (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) A₀ = π × 10²/4 = 78.54 mm².
In the elastic region, σ = 20 000/78.54 = 254.6 MPa and ε = 0.060/50.0 = 0.0012, so E = 254.6/0.0012 = 212 000 MPa ≈ 212 GPa. This is consistent with the 200–210 GPa expected for steel.
0.2% proof stress = 28 000/78.54 = 357 MPa.
UTS = 40 000/78.54 = 509 MPa.
Percentage elongation = (61.0 − 50.0)/50.0 × 100 = 22%.
Reduction of area = (1 − (6.5/10.0)²) × 100 = (1 − 0.4225) × 100 = 57.8%.
Comment: an elongation of over 20% and a reduction of area near 58% show a ductile steel that will neck and deform visibly before fracture. The ratio UTS/proof ≈ 1.43 shows useful strain hardening, which is desirable for structural steel because it spreads yielding and gives warning before failure.

(b) Fast fracture occurs when Yσ√(πa) = K_IC, so a_c = (1/π)(K_IC/(Yσ))².
Yσ = 1.12 × 200 = 224 MPa, and K_IC/(Yσ) = 60/224 = 0.2679 √m.
a_c = 0.2679²/π = 0.07175/π = 0.0228 m ≈ 22.8 mm.
An edge crack deeper than about 23 mm would cause fast fracture at this stress. In practice inspection intervals are set so that fatigue cracks are found well before they grow to this size.

(c) Cycles to failure:
N(100) = 1.024 × 10¹²/100³ = 1.024 × 10⁶
N(60) = 1.024 × 10¹²/60³ = 1.024 × 10¹²/216 000 = 4.74 × 10⁶
Annual damage D = 3 × 10⁴/1.024 × 10⁶ + 1.5 × 10⁵/4.74 × 10⁶ = 0.0293 + 0.0316 = 0.0609.
Miner's rule predicts failure when the cumulative damage reaches 1, so the life is 1/0.0609 ≈ 16.4 years.
Miner's rule assumes damage accumulates linearly and is independent of load order. Real sequences (for example a few large cycles early on) can give shorter or longer lives, so design codes apply partial factors and detail-specific S–N curves to such estimates.

(d) Ferritic structural steels are BCC and show a ductile-to-brittle transition: below a transition temperature, Charpy energy drops sharply and a crack (from a weld defect or a fatigue crack such as in (c)) can run in a brittle way with little warning. An exposed UK bridge can see sub-zero temperatures in winter, and welded thick plates are especially vulnerable. Specifying a sub-grade such as J2 (at least 27 J absorbed in a Charpy test at −20 °C) ensures that the steel remains tough at the lowest temperatures it is likely to meet. Thicker plates or colder sites may need a tougher grade.
